svg.title: Publishing the source of a private project, without the parts that must stay private: Publication keeps its safety promises from source selection to repeated releases
svg.text: Publishing the source of a private project, without the
Scenario: Publication keeps its safety promises from source selection to repeated releases
Exactly the committed files, or nothing
Publication runs only when asked, and only after a real scan
Tokens and setup failures stay safe
Releases on a real public project on GitLab

g.text: Given a throwaway source repository whose files are approved for publication
A real Git repository built for this story, in a real terminal. It tracks src/message.txt and the publication's own
files under .config/publication. Its ignore file, .gitignore, also matches src/message.txt: the last chapter comes back
to that.
The allowlist lets src/ and .gitignore leave, the manifest says both were approved, and publication-owner is the one
person who may approve. The .env file holds the settings: a public repository next door, two throwaway tokens, and
fixture-forge, the stand-in for GitLab's API. Every other repository in this story is a copy of this one with one thing
changed.
Then export copies the committed bytes, past a local smudge filter and into a folder whose
name starts with a dash
This copy adds -public/message.txt, in a folder whose name starts with a dash, which a careless shell command would read
as an option. It also sets a smudge filter, a local Git setting that rewrites a file when Git writes it to disk: the
working copy of src/message.txt says UNCOMMITTED CONTENT.
The export writes what would be published into ../snapshot and prints 3, the number of files. Both files there hold the
committed text: the filter changed nothing, and the dash folder arrived whole. The task is this repository's own name
for the line below, which any project with the publication can run.
And the dry run names and refuses a symbolic link, an LFS pointer and a
missing framework denylist
Three copies, three commits the publication cannot copy faithfully. src/host is a symbolic
link (Git mode 120000). src/large.txt is a Git LFS pointer, a small text file standing in for
a large one. The third commit deletes denylist.base, the framework's own list of files that
never leave.
task publication:check, the dry run, refuses all three and names the file each time, instead
of listing it as publishable.
Then publication does nothing when it is switched off, or when CI starts
it outside its manual or tag job
Three runs of task publication:publish, each told not to publish: switched off with
TASK_PUBLICATION_ENABLED=false, then two runs that look like a CI job (CI=true) set to
publish only from a manual job, or only from a tag pipeline. Each says why in one line and
stops.
The last two commands check both sides: the public repository has 0 commits, and the stand-in
forge received 0 requests.
And the dry run never contacts the forge: it passes offline and refuses
an absent ref instead of fetching it
In this copy, origin, the address Git fetches from, points at the stand-in forge: a fetch
would show up in its request log. The dry run lists the 2 files it would publish, and says
the owner's signature is only checked when publishing.
Asked for a branch that does not exist, it answers No such ref instead of fetching it. The
request log is still empty.
And publication refuses to skip the secret scan, and stops before the push when Git cannot
read a file
TASK_PUBLICATION_SCAN=done is not a mode: nobody can tell the publication that the secret scan already happened. It
refuses.
The next two copies run a stand-in git, printed on the card, ahead of the real one. In export-fails, every read of a
file's contents fails: the publication stops before the scan, which never ran (0 lines in scan.log). In index-fails, the
reads fail only after the scan passed (1 line): the publication still stops, and says Nothing was pushed. Both public
repositories have 0 commits.
Then only an owner's answer that names the current manifest and was not edited afterwards
approves publication, and approval asks the owner again
For this copy, the stand-in forge answers with the three threads of discussions.json, all resolved by publication-owner.
One is about spelling. One names a manifest of zeros, an older list. One names this manifest, the hash on the first
line, but its question was edited after it was resolved: updated_at comes after resolved_at.
None of them counts, so task publication:publish refuses: the approved list carries no owner signature. task
publication:approve then asks again on merge request !1, and the request log ends with the POST that asks the new
question.
And approval fails loudly when the forge refuses every request, or only the sign-off thread
This copy adds src/new.txt, a file nobody approved, so task publication:approve has to open a merge request. The
stand-in forge is told to refuse every API request, then only the POST of the sign-off thread.
Both runs fail and say so: The forge refused the approval request. Nothing was approved. The request log shows where
each run stopped, marked 403, the code a forge answers when it refuses: at the very first request, then at the very last
one.
Then neither token shows up, in process arguments or in the refusal of a target URL that
carries one
Here git, curl, sed and jq are stand-ins that write every argument they receive to argv.log, then run the real tool. The
publication succeeds. The log holds the clone and the push, and neither throwaway token from .env: grep counts 0.
The last command puts a token inside the public repository's URL. The dry run refuses that URL, and its answer does not
repeat the token.
And setup keeps the working token and CI variables when the forge refuses their replacement
task publication:init is the one-time setup. It asks two questions, answered with Enter, then replaces the project's
token and stores the new one in two CI/CD variables. The stand-in forge refuses the new token, then, on the second run,
the update of the variables.
Both runs fail and say so. The request log has no DELETE: the token CI still uses was not revoked, and no variable was
deleted. .env.dist records the destination, but publication is not switched on.
And setup started from an onboarding branch turns on the discussion gate
and schedules the main branch
This copy sits on a branch called onboarding. Setup succeeds, and its own lines say what it
changed: GitLab now requires all discussions to be resolved before merging, and a nightly
schedule runs on main, not on onboarding.
The request log tells the same story, and one more thing: the old token is deleted only after
its replacement is stored.
When the first release is published to an empty public project on GitLab
The last copy publishes to a real public project on the test GitLab, empty until now. Its ignore file still matches
src/*.txt.
The publication is approved, pushes 2 files, and names the release after the source commit, since no tag exists yet.
Then the public project holds every approved file, even one its ignore file matches
GitLab's page for src/message.txt in the public project. The Files panel lists .gitignore and src/message.txt, the two
approved files, and the file holds the committed text. Its one commit, publish <source-commit-1>, was made by DevSecOps
Toolbox.
The ignore file did not hold it back: the publication copies what Git tracks, whatever a working copy would ignore.
When a tag is added to that release later, then a new release with the same files is
published twice
The developer tags the commit already published as 1.0.0: the public repository is already up to date, so only the tag
is added. Then an empty commit tagged 1.0.1, with the same files: it gets its own public commit. Publishing 1.0.1 again
changes nothing.
Then the late tag sits on the commit already published, and the new release has its own
commit and tag
GitLab's Tags page of the public project, sorted by name. 1.0.0 sits on the first commit, still named after the source
commit it published. 1.0.1 sits on its own commit, publish 1.0.1.
Two tags on two commits: the late tag made no commit, and the retry added nothing.
And a public tag that already names another commit stops the next release, and the main
branch stays where it was
Somebody has tagged the public project 1.0.2 by hand on GitLab, on its current commit: the first command lists it. The
developer then changes the source and tags it 1.0.2 as well.
The publication refuses: the public tag 1.0.2 already identifies another commit. It pushes nothing, so the main branch
of the public project is on <public-commit-2> before and after.
